desc:
A pattern p is a sequence of items. Each item is a lowercase letter or the character . (which matches any single letter), optionally followed by a repeat range written as {lo,hi}, where lo and hi are single digits with lo ≤ hi. An item without a range matches exactly one character; an item with a range matches between lo and hi characters (inclusive), each of which must be matched by the letter or the dot.

Return true if the pattern matches the whole string s.

s = "abbc",   p = "ab{1,3}c"  ->  true
s = "ac",     p = "ab{1,3}c"  ->  false  (b must appear at least once)
s = "abbbbc", p = "ab{1,3}c"  ->  false  (b may appear at most three times)
s = "",       p = "a{0,2}"    ->  true
s = "xyz",    p = ".{2,4}"     ->  true
constraints: p is well formed: items are letters or ., each optionally followed by exactly one {lo,hi} with single digits 0 ≤ lo ≤ hi ≤ 9
hints: A recursive search that tries every allowed count for each item can blow up. Think about which positions of s are reachable after processing the first few items.

Keep the set of all text positions that can be reached after the items processed so far. For one item with range {lo,hi}, repeatedly step over characters that match, and collect the positions reached after at least lo and at most hi steps.

The reachable positions fit in a bitmask over 0..n. Precompute for every letter a mask of the positions where s has that letter; one matching step is (cur & mask) << 1. The answer is whether bit n is set at the end.
editorial: Let R be the set of positions i such that the items processed so far can match exactly s[:i]. Start with R = {0}. For an item matching between lo and hi characters, repeat up to hi times: from the current frontier keep the positions whose next character matches the item and move one step to the right. The new R is the union of the frontiers after lo, lo+1, ..., hi steps (and the starting frontier itself if lo = 0). The string matches if position n is in the final set.

Doing this with Python integers as bitsets makes every step a few big-integer operations on 3,000 bits instead of a loop over positions: shift left by one to advance, and AND with a precomputed mask to filter on the letter. The cost is about 9 · items bitset operations. The same DP can be written as a table dp[item][pos] with a loop over the counts, which is O(items · n · 9). Plain backtracking is exponential on patterns such as repeated .{0,9}.
